title: Responders in Türkiye used xView2 machine-learning damage maps after the 6 February 2023 earthquakes
summary: After the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, xView2, a machine-learning model that grades building damage in satellite images, gave responders maps that UN rescue teams used in Adıyaman.
account: In 2019 the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute sponsored and developed xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. Partners included Microsoft and the University of California, Berkeley. It uses machine learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors who include Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with Türkiye's Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD) to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from 7 to 9 February 2023. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. MIT Technology Review reported on xView2 on 20 February 2023. Gupta told the magazine that at least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said that it helped workers find damaged areas that they were unaware of. He said that AFAD, the World Bank, the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) and the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said that the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article gives 9 February 2023 as the first date with usable images. The technical report that it links includes 7 February imagery for Islahiye and 9 February imagery for the other three cities. The article says that the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states that its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. No responder statement that describes a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources. On 27 October 2025 researchers from Stanford University and Direct Relief published in PLOS Digital Health an outside test of the Microsoft model built on xBD, the dataset behind xView2. Among 38 hospitals and dialysis centers in three cities, the model found 42.86% of the damaged facilities and correctly cleared 93.55% of the undamaged ones. The authors conclude that such models cannot yet replace ground surveys. Direct Relief's article of 10 December 2025 describes this research study on Microsoft and Google models. It does not describe a response decision.
purpose: Rapid building-damage assessment from pre- and post-event satellite imagery for humanitarian assistance and disaster response. This use was that purpose.
system: xView2 building damage assessment models (semantic segmentation on satellite imagery, trained on the xBD dataset)
developer: US Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) with Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute; research partners Microsoft AI for Good and UC Berkeley
deployer: UN INSARAG (search and rescue ground teams in Adıyaman); AFAD, World Bank, IFRC and WFP (per the developer's account); Microsoft AI for Good delivered estimates to AFAD (per Microsoft)
location: Adıyaman and four cities in southeast Türkiye including Kahramanmaraş (Marash)

ratings.reason: No individual rescue or beneficiary is attributed to the maps in any cited source.

The developer and a World Bank specialist report that responders received building-level damage maps within hours or minutes, where such an assessment would typically take weeks. The developer reports that teams found damaged areas that they had been unaware of. No responding agency gives its own account.
No downstream effect on rescues, shelter siting or reconstruction is documented. The maps covered part of the affected zone after imagery became usable on 9 February 2023.

data.retained_case_account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article gives February 9, 2023, as the first usable-image date. However, the linked technical report includes February 7 imagery for Islahiye and February 9 imagery for the other three cities. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from February 7 to February 9. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.

fields.account: In 2019 the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute sponsored and developed xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. Partners included Microsoft and the University of California, Berkeley. It uses machine learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors who include Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with Türkiye's Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD) to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from 7 to 9 February 2023. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. MIT Technology Review reported on xView2 on 20 February 2023. Gupta told the magazine that at least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said that it helped workers find damaged areas that they were unaware of. He said that AFAD, the World Bank, the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) and the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said that the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article gives 9 February 2023 as the first date with usable images. The technical report that it links includes 7 February imagery for Islahiye and 9 February imagery for the other three cities. The article says that the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states that its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. No responder statement that describes a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources. On 27 October 2025 researchers from Stanford University and Direct Relief published in PLOS Digital Health an outside test of the Microsoft model built on xBD, the dataset behind xView2. Among 38 hospitals and dialysis centers in three cities, the model found 42.86% of the damaged facilities and correctly cleared 93.55% of the undamaged ones. The authors conclude that such models cannot yet replace ground surveys. Direct Relief's article of 10 December 2025 describes this research study on Microsoft and Google models. It does not describe a response decision.

ratings.reason: No individual rescue or beneficiary is attributed to the maps in any cited source.

The developer and a World Bank specialist report that responders received building-level damage maps within hours or minutes, where such an assessment would typically take weeks. The developer reports that teams found damaged areas that they had been unaware of. No responding agency gives its own account.
No downstream effect on rescues, shelter siting or reconstruction is documented. The maps covered part of the affected zone after imagery became usable on 9 February 2023.
